title: Binary Classification
body:
[[Stratification]]
[[MNIST]]

---

[[Classification]] with exactly two labels, positive and negative. It matters out of proportion to
how simple it is, because **the entire evaluation vocabulary is defined here**: [[True Positive]],
[[False Positive]], [[Sensitivity]], [[Specificity]], the [[Confusion Matrix]] itself. Multi-class
metrics are built by reducing to this case one class at a time.

Two labels means **one number suffices**. The model outputs $p = P(\text{positive})$ and the
negative probability is $1-p$, so the [[Output Layer]] needs a single [[Sigmoid]] unit rather than
a softmax over $k$. That is what [[Logistic Regression]] fits, and the distribution being fitted is
a [[Bernoulli Distribution]]. The matching loss is [[Log Loss]].

**Which class you call "positive" is a choice, and it is not neutral.** It decides which cell is a
[[False Positive]] and which a [[False Negative]], and therefore what [[Sensitivity]] measures. The
convention is that positive is the rare, interesting, or costly-to-miss class: disease present,
message is spam, transaction is fraud.

Evan's two links above are the reason it is not trivial in practice. **[[Stratification]]** because
the interesting binary problems are imbalanced, and an unstratified split can leave a test set with
almost no positives in it. **[[MNIST]]** because the course's first classifier is the binary
reduction of it: "is this a 5, yes or no", trained with [[SGD Classification]], before the
ten-class version.

Any multi-class problem reduces to a set of these, which is how the metrics generalise:
one-versus-rest fits $k$ binary classifiers, one per class against everything else.
